newsitem.title: USA: Group says Democrats unfair to U.S. subsidiaries.
newsitem.headline: Group says Democrats unfair to U.S. subsidiaries.

text.p: Citing the millions of jobs created by foreign investment in the United States, a trade group on Wednesday criticised efforts to limit U.S. political participation by these companies through campaign donations.

The Organisation for International Investment said the Democratic National Committee discriminated against millions of people when it decided recently it would no longer accept contributions from U.S. subsidiaries of foreign firms.

"The actions taken by the DNC, in our view, discriminate unfairly and unjustly against American workers," the group's chairman, Richard Goldstein, told a news conference called to herald an increase in foreign investment in the United States.

The DNC has returned large sums of money to contributors after reports that it improperly solicited funds from foreign business interests with a stake in U.S. trade policy. The returned money included $425,000 from Indonesians who lived in the United States and had ties to Indonesia's Lippo Group conglomerate as well as a $250,000 contribution that was given back after it was determined it came from a South Korean company, Cheong Am, and not its U.S. subsidiary.

But Goldstein said the "arbitrary" nature of the DNC's decision affected many Americans, not just foreigners. He said international investment in the United States was providing jobs to 4.9 million workers, more than double the number of such jobs the investment created back in 1980.

"Discriminating against the rights of workers, employees, on the basis of whom their employer happens to be strikes many of us as un-American, not the type of thing that this country stands for," added Goldstein, the president of Unilever United States Inc., whose parent firm is a Dutch-U.K. conglomerate.

"The DNC policy was aiming at Lippo bank contributions, but they shot MCI as well," another trade group official said, referring to the pending merger of MCI Communications Corp. with British Telecommunications PLC.

U.S. subsidiaries of foreign firms paid $8.2 billion in federal taxes in 1993, the most recent year for which the data was available, Goldstein said. The average monthly wage at these companies was close to 26 percent higher than that paid to workers at all U.S. businesses, he said.

Todd Malan, the trade group's executive director, said there was little doubt about the need for campaign finance reform but that it should be non-discriminatory, such as banning all "soft money" outside current limits on giving, or banning political action committees that make donations.
"They shouldn't pick and choose" who can donate, he said.

The Republicans have not followed the DNC's example in renouncing donations from U.S. subsidiaries of foreign-owned companies. Neither have Democratic committees that raise money for congressional campaigns, limiting the impact of the DNC's decision looking ahead to the non-presidential election year in 1998.
